title: Can a Language Model Write the Weights? An Empirical Study of LLM-Written Scoring Networks for Column Generation and MILP Branching, with a Bus-Driver Scheduling Application

target_networks.name: branching scoring MLP (one linear layer or one ReLU layer of width 6, stored as JSON)
column-generation arc / label / ng-neighbourhood scoring networks

domain: operations research (column generation, MILP branching, crew scheduling)
tasks_benchmarks: synthetic set cover / combinatorial auction / facility location / independent set (Gasse et al. 2019 settings)
MARTA GTFS bus-driver scheduling (32 held-out garages)

headline_result.text: LLM-written branching rules cut solve time to 0.63x of SCIP's default on 32 held-out bus-scheduling instances, but SCIP's plain pseudocost rule did the same (ratio 0.99, p = 0.19); the only gain attributable to the written weights was 0.37x time on synthetic independent set.
headline_result.quote: the LLM-written rules took 0.63× the default’s time on 32 held-out instances (p < 10−4 ) — but SCIP’s own plain pseudocost rule did exactly as well (ratio 0.99, p = 0.19).

key_claims.claim: In column generation for VRPTW no lever gave a material gain; the LLM-written arc scorer tied the classical reduced-cost rule.
key_claims.quote: the LLM-written arc scorer ties the classical reduced-cost rule (time ratio 1.02 over 34 instances;

key_claims.claim: On synthetic independent set the LLM-written rule v1 was faster than SCIP's default on all 18 instances, with a time ratio of 0.37.
key_claims.quote: On independent set, v1 is faster on all 18 instances, with a geometric-mean time ratio of 0.37 (p = 7.6 × 10−6 )

key_claims.claim: With the same features, hand-written weights matched or beat gradient-trained imitation-of-strong-branching weights in 3 of 4 settings.
key_claims.quote: With the same 7 features, hand-written weights match or beat weights trained by imitation of strong branching in 3 of 4 settings

key_claims.claim: The synthetic rule did not generalise: on MIPLIB 2017 it solved fewer instances than SCIP's default.
key_claims.quote: The rule is family-specific: on 39 MIPLIB 2017 instances it solves 19 vs 24

key_claims.claim: In the real-data application the whole speed-up was reproduced by a one-line solver configuration change, so the gain came from being cheap rather than from what the LLM wrote.
key_claims.quote: the measured speed-up of about 37% was real but was entirely reproduced by switching SCIP to its plain pseudocost rule, a one-line configuration change.

limitations_stated.text: Instance sets are small and the MARTA labour rules and garage grouping are synthetic.
limitations_stated.quote: (iv) Instance sets are small (8–40 per comparison). (v) The MARTA labour rules and garage grouping are synthetic.

limitations_stated.text: The same AI wrote the weights, ran the analysis and wrote the paper (circularity).
limitations_stated.quote: The same AI wrote the weights, ran the analysis and wrote this paper; to limit this, every number is produced by a script from logs that are released

limitations_stated.text: The trained baseline is deliberately small, not a reproduction of the Gasse et al. graph network.
limitations_stated.quote: This is a deliberately small baseline (same 7 features, 2k nodes), not a reproduction of the graph network of Gasse et al. [2019].

notes_for_review: Applies WSP (LLM writes small scoring networks from forward-pass diagnostics) to exact OR algorithms, with paired comparisons, practice/test splits and Wilcoxon tests. Its key contribution is the cheap-baseline control: the main application gain is fully matched by SCIP's built-in pseudocost rule, so the gain is not attributable to WSP. The paper, code and weights were all generated by Claude Opus 5.5 under human direction, which the author discloses. Evidence is careful but on small instance sets with single runs per instance.
